nameStory: This lichen carries the name of Bérenger, likely a 19th-century botanist or collector who first studied this species. The genus name Mycobilimbia hints at its fungal nature (myco-) and its crusty, patchy appearance (bilimbia refers to a type of lichen with small, round fruiting bodies). Like many scientific discoveries, it honors someone who contributed to our understanding of these fascinating dual organisms.
description: Berenger's mycobilimbia is a crustose lichen that forms thin, crusty patches on rock surfaces. This organism is actually two living things in one - a fungus and algae working together in partnership. It appears as grayish to whitish patches that seem almost painted onto stone surfaces. Individual patches typically spread only a few inches across, creating modest colonies that blend subtly with their rocky homes.

idTips.label: Crusty rock patches
idTips.description: Forms thin, crusty coatings on rock that feel slightly rough to the touch, like fine sandpaper adhered to stone

idTips.label: Grayish-white color
idTips.description: Displays pale gray to whitish tones that may appear almost chalky in bright sunlight

idTips.label: Small fruiting bodies
idTips.description: Produces tiny, dark spots (apothecia) that feel like pinhead-sized bumps scattered across the surface

idTips.label: Rock substrate preference
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found growing directly on bare rock surfaces, never on bark or soil

idTips.label: Thin growth form
idTips.description: Creates very flat patches that seem to merge seamlessly with the rock surface, rarely more than paper-thin

habitat: Look for this rare lichen on exposed rock faces and boulders in New England's mountainous regions and rocky coastal areas. It prefers hard, non-calcareous rocks like granite or quartzite in areas with clean air and minimal pollution. Given its single recorded observation in New England, it's likely found in remote, pristine locations away from urban development.

seasonality.spring: Emerging from winter dormancy, the lichen may show renewed growth and slightly brighter coloration as moisture returns.
seasonality.summer: Most active growth period when warm temperatures and occasional moisture promote expansion of the crusty patches.
seasonality.fall: Continues photosynthesis during mild weather, with fruiting bodies potentially most visible during this season.
seasonality.winter: Enters dormancy but remains visible on rocks, often appearing more muted gray against snow-covered surfaces.

funFact: This lichen is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only once in scientific records - making anyone who finds it again a genuine contributor to regional biodiversity knowledge, like discovering a needle in a haystack the size of six states!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other gray crustose lichens on rocks, but most common rock lichens in New England form thicker, more obvious patches or have distinctly different colors like the orange or yellow of Caloplaca species.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of this species in New England (only one recorded observation) suggests it may be at the edge of its geographic range here, or requires very specific environmental conditions that are uncommon in our region.
compareHints: Since no other Mycobilimbia species are recorded in New England, compare it with other members of the Lecideaceae family like Lecidea lichens, which typically form thicker, more prominent crusty patches and often have more distinctly raised, black fruiting bodies. Berenger's mycobilimbia tends to be thinner and more seamlessly integrated with the rock surface.
